title: x y z qu
goal: Read and spell x, y, z, and the qu spelling; the alphabet's sounds are now complete (all 26 letters covered across L1.02–L1.12).
newToday: x (usually says /ks/, two sounds in one letter), y (as a consonant, /j/, at the start of a word — its vowel jobs come in Level 3), z, qu (always together, says /kw/) — **one new grapheme per sitting**.
review: j, v, w; words jam, van, wet.
heartLine: have, go (taught in the final combined sitting).
time: five sittings — A (~12 min), B (~10 min), C (~10 min), D (~10 min), E (~25–30 min).

A.text: Sam has a fox. Sam has a box. The fox naps in the box. Sam has six pups. Go, fox, go!

B.text: Dan has a box. Nat has a box. Dan and Nat fix a van. Nat quits at six. Go, Nat, go!

questions: What did the main character have, and where did it end up?
What time does the action happen in Track B?
Think: "has" says its final s like /z/, just like "is" did back in L1.03 — can you think of another word ending in s that might say /z/ the same way?

listen.title: All 26, At Last
listen.passage: Every single letter of the English alphabet has now had its own proper introduction — some of them, like c and k, even share a job. It took twelve lessons to get here, on purpose: rushing through all 26 letters in a week or two sounds efficient, but it means most of them never get practiced enough to become automatic. From here, nothing new needs to be "discovered" — the next lessons are about combining these same 26 letters in cleverer and cleverer ways: two letters making one sound, sounds joining into longer words, and patterns repeating across hundreds of different words once you know what to look for.

tier2.def: happening without needing to think about it carefully each time, because it's been practiced so much.
tier2.full: happening without needing to think about it carefully each time, because it's been practiced so much. "Reading familiar words becomes automatic after enough practice." "Braking for a red light should be automatic for a driver." Your turn: name something you do automatically now that used to take real effort.

tier2.def: putting two or more things together to make something new.
tier2.full: putting two or more things together to make something new. "Combining flour and water makes dough." "This lesson is about combining letters in new ways." Your turn: what's something good that comes from combining two things?

questions: Why does the passage say rushing through all 26 letters quickly would actually be worse, not better?
What does the passage say comes next, now that all 26 letters are taught?

warm.text: flash j, v, w. Read 3 review words: jam, van, wet.

hear.text: /ks/ — x is unusual: it's really two sounds squeezed into one letter, /k/ then /s/, like the end of "box."

meet.text: "This says /ks/" (x — usually at the *end* of a word). Demonstrate slowly: say /k/ then /s/ separately, then squeeze them together fast, so the learner hears it's genuinely two sounds, not a mystery third sound.

spell.text: say /ks/ → write **x**. Segment and write "box" (three sounds: /b/ /o/ /ks/ — note x counts as the last "chunk" even though it's two sounds).

mini.text: x on sight 5/5; blend the 5 words above at ≥4/5.

warm.text: flash x. Read 3 review words: box, fox, six.

hear.text: /j/ (consonant y) — tongue humps up toward the roof of the mouth, like the start of "yes."

meet.text: "This says /j/" (y — at the *start* of a word only, for now; y's vowel jobs come in Level 3).

mini.text: y on sight 5/5; blend the 3 words above at ≥3/3 (a smaller set — consonant-y has few word-initial CVC partners, which is fine).

warm.text: flash y. Read 3 review words: yes, yak, yum.

hear.text: /z/ — like /s/ but voiced (buzzing), the start of "zip."

mini.text: z on sight 5/5; blend the 2 words above at ≥2/2.

warm.text: flash z. Read 2 review words: zip, zap.

hear.text: /kw/ — q is never alone in English; it always partners with u, and together they say /kw/, like the start of "quiz."

meet.text: "These two always go together and say /kw/" (qu). "q never goes anywhere without u in English — they're a package."

mini.text: qu on sight 2/2; blend the 2 words above at ≥2/2.

sittings.title: x, y, z, qu together: heart words, Read it, Check (~25–30 min)

warm.text: flash x, y, z, qu; blend 5 mixed words spanning all four: box, yes, zip, quiz, fix.

spell.text: 1. Segment and write: "quiz." 2. Sentence dictation: **"Go, fox, go!"** (Go: heart word; fox: /f/ /o/ /ks/.)

heart.note: h (✓), a (✓), v (✓) are all regular. The final e usually signals "make the vowel before it say its long name" (a pattern called silent-e, taught properly in Level 3) — if that rule applied here, "have" would say "hayv." **It doesn't** — it stays short, /hæv/. **Heart part: the silent e breaks its own future rule in this one very common word.** Say: "you'll learn the real silent-e rule soon; this word is the famous exception to it."

g (✓) is regular. The o says a long /oʊ/ here (like "go," "so," "no" — a pattern called an open syllable, taught properly in Level 3, L3.5). **Heart part: the "o" says its long sound, not the short one you know.**
